title: Isolation levels and anomalies
scopeHtml: Scope: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom reads, write skew, Postgres levels and SSI with two-session SQL examples, choosing a level.

notes.title: Why isolation levels exist
notes.html:
Isolation decides how much one transaction can see of another transaction's work while both are running. Perfect isolation (serializable: the result equals some one-at-a-time order) is the safest but the most expensive, so SQL defines weaker levels that allow certain "anomalies" in exchange for speed and fewer conflicts.

The SQL standard lists four levels by which anomalies they forbid:

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Write skew
Read Uncommitted allowed allowed allowed allowed
Read Committed no allowed allowed allowed
Repeatable Read no no allowed (standard) allowed
Serializable no no no no

Postgres reality: Read Uncommitted behaves exactly like Read Committed (no dirty reads ever). Postgres's Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation, so it also blocks phantoms, but still allows write skew. Only Serializable (SSI) blocks write skew.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;   -- per transaction
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;      -- 'read committed' by default

Industry examples. Postgres default is Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB default is Repeatable Read. Oracle has no Repeatable Read (Read Committed or Serializable, which is really snapshot isolation). CockroachDB and Spanner give serializable by default.

Decision gravity. The level is a per-transaction setting, so it is reversible. The design choice that is hard to undo is writing code that silently depends on the default. Document which level each critical path assumes.

Everyday analogy. Several people editing a shared whiteboard: do you see someone's scribbles as they write (dirty), or only when they step away (committed), or a frozen photo taken when you started (snapshot)?

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the standard's table as if every database follows it. Postgres and Oracle differ.
  • Saying Postgres default is Repeatable Read (that is MySQL).

notes.title: Dirty read
notes.html:
A dirty read is seeing data another transaction has written but not yet committed. If that transaction rolls back, you acted on data that never existed.

Postgres never allows it. Two-session example on a table accounts(id=1, balance=100):

Session A                           Session B
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=500
  WHERE id=1;
                                    BEGIN;
                                    SELECT balance FROM accounts
                                      WHERE id=1;   -- sees 100 in Postgres
                                                    -- (a dirty-read DB would show 500)
ROLLBACK;

In a database with true Read Uncommitted (SQL Server with READ UNCOMMITTED or NOLOCK hints), B would have seen 500, then A rolls back and 500 never existed.

Real incident pattern. SQL Server reports built with WITH (NOLOCK) showing revenue figures that included orders later cancelled, or rows read twice during page splits. In Postgres this class of bug cannot occur.

Everyday analogy. Reading a colleague's unsent email draft and acting on it, then they delete it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED gives dirty reads in Postgres. It silently upgrades to Read Committed.
  • Confusing dirty read with stale read; stale data is committed, merely old.

notes.title: Non-repeatable read
notes.html:
A non-repeatable read happens when you read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because someone committed a change in between. Read Committed allows it: each STATEMENT gets a fresh snapshot.

Session A (Read Committed)          Session B
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts
  WHERE id=1;          -- 100
                                    UPDATE accounts SET balance=50
                                      WHERE id=1;   -- autocommit
SELECT balance FROM accounts
  WHERE id=1;          -- 50  (changed!)
COMMIT;

With BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, A's snapshot is taken at its first statement and both reads return 100.

The Read Committed twist: UPDATE and DELETE re-check the row after waiting for a lock. If A runs UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id=1 while B holds an uncommitted update on the row, A waits, then re-reads the NEW committed row (EvalPlanQual) and applies its change to the latest version. That is why atomic balance = balance - 10 is safe in Read Committed but SELECT then UPDATE balance = 90 (lost update) is not.

Worked example (lost update). App reads balance 100, computes 90 in code, writes 90. Another app does the same with 20 off, writes 80. Final 80 instead of 70. Fixes: atomic UPDATE expression, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic version column (file 08), or Repeatable Read (second writer errors with could not serialize access due to concurrent update).

Everyday analogy. Checking the price tag, then finding it changed at the till seconds later.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing statement-level vs transaction-level snapshots.
  • Thinking Read Committed protects read-modify-write cycles in app code. It does not.

notes.title: Phantom read
notes.html:
A phantom is a new row appearing (or a row disappearing) in the result of the same query run twice, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows. Non-repeatable read is about a row you already saw; phantom is about the SET of rows.

Session A (Read Committed)          Session B
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
  WHERE day = '2026-11-09';   -- 10
                                    INSERT INTO orders(day) VALUES ('2026-11-09');
                                    -- committed
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
  WHERE day = '2026-11-09';   -- 11  phantom

Row-level locks cannot stop phantoms because the new row did not exist to lock. The standard needed Serializable to prevent them; many databases use gap/predicate locks (InnoDB next-key locks in Repeatable Read). Postgres Repeatable Read prevents them via the snapshot: A never sees B's insert because B committed after A's snapshot. That is stronger than the standard demands.

Industry examples. InnoDB at Repeatable Read still shows phantoms to locking reads (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE sees the latest data) while plain reads use the snapshot; a source of subtle bugs when migrating between MySQL and Postgres.

Everyday analogy. Counting the people in a room, then recounting and finding a new person who walked in.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up phantom and non-repeatable read.
  • Claiming Postgres Repeatable Read allows phantoms (the standard allows it; Postgres does not).

notes.title: Write skew
notes.html:
Write skew is when two transactions read overlapping data, each decides something is safe, then each writes a DIFFERENT row, and together they break a rule neither broke alone. Each write touches a different row, so there is no write-write conflict and snapshot isolation (Postgres Repeatable Read) does not notice.

Classic: a hospital requires at least one doctor on call. Alice and Bob are both on call.

Session A (Repeatable Read)         Session B (Repeatable Read)
BEGIN;                              BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors
  WHERE on_call;       -- 2
                                    SELECT count(*) FROM doctors
                                      WHERE on_call;       -- 2
UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false
  WHERE name='Alice';
                                    UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false
                                      WHERE name='Bob';
COMMIT;                             COMMIT;   -- both succeed
-- result: zero doctors on call, rule broken

Fixes, from cheapest:

  1. Run both at SERIALIZABLE; Postgres aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001 (retry it).
  2. Lock the rows you read: SELECT ... FROM doctors WHERE on_call FOR UPDATE, so the second waits.
  3. Lock a single "guard" row (e.g. the ward) so the transactions conflict.
  4. Make the rule a constraint (e.g. an EXCLUDE or trigger), where possible.

Industry examples. Double-booking a meeting room, selling the last seat twice, two users claiming the same unique username when checked in code only, overspending a shared budget.

Everyday analogy. Two flatmates each see "there is milk in the fridge, so I will drink my cup", but there was only one cup left.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Repeatable Read is enough for "check then act" logic.
  • Forgetting retry logic: Serializable requires the app to retry 40001.

notes.title: Serializable in Postgres (SSI)
notes.html:
Serializable means the outcome equals running the transactions one at a time in some order. Postgres implements it with Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): transactions run on snapshots (no extra blocking), and Postgres tracks "read-write dependencies" with lightweight SIREAD predicate locks. When it finds a dangerous cycle (two consecutive rw-edges, the signature of write skew) it aborts one transaction with ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ... reads and writes ...
COMMIT;   -- may fail with SQLSTATE 40001: retry the WHOLE transaction

Retry loop (Python-ish):

for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        with conn.transaction():          # BEGIN SERIALIZABLE
            do_work(conn)
        break
    except SerializationFailure:           # sqlstate 40001
        sleep(0.01 * 2**attempt)           # backoff + jitter in real code

Practical notes:

  • False positives are possible (it errs on the safe side), so rate of retries matters; measure it.
  • Predicate locks live in shared memory (max_pred_locks_per_transaction, default 64) and can escalate from tuple to page to relation level, raising false aborts.
  • Long read-only transactions can use SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY DEFERRABLE, which waits for a safe snapshot then never aborts.
  • Do not mix levels carelessly: for full protection all transactions that take part in the invariant must run SERIALIZABLE.

Decision gravity. Serializable plus a retry wrapper is a pragmatic way to get correctness without designing locks for every path. Alternative: explicit FOR UPDATE locks (predictable, but you must remember them everywhere). Reversible per transaction, but every caller needs retry code, so adopting it late touches a lot.

Industry examples. CockroachDB and Spanner are serializable by default; their clients must retry. Postgres SSI is from the 2008 research by Cahill et al., shipped in 9.1.

Everyday analogy. A referee who lets everyone play simultaneously, then blows the whistle on the one move that cannot be explained by playing in turn.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Serializable without retries.
  • Thinking Serializable means "table locks". In Postgres it does not block; it aborts.

notes.title: Choosing a level and testing it
notes.html:
Default to Read Committed, use atomic SQL for simple cases, and move specific critical transactions to Repeatable Read or Serializable.

Decision guide:

Situation Choice
Single-statement updates (SET x = x + 1) Read Committed is fine
Report needing one consistent view over many queries Repeatable Read, READ ONLY
Check-then-act on a set (booking, quotas, on-call) Serializable with retry, or FOR UPDATE
Read-modify-write on one row FOR UPDATE or optimistic version column

Worked example. Seat booking with 5,000 req/s at launch for 100,000 seats. Using Serializable with retries on a hot row yields retries storming (say 30 to 50% aborts, numbers illustrative). A cheaper design: UPDATE seats SET holder = $u WHERE id = $s AND holder IS NULL RETURNING id; an atomic conditional update that works in Read Committed with zero retries, and the row count tells you if you won.

UPDATE seats SET holder = 42
WHERE id = 7 AND holder IS NULL
RETURNING id;      -- 1 row = booked, 0 rows = someone else got it

Testing concurrency. Reproduce with two psql sessions, or a script using pg_sleep to widen the race window; for automated tests, use two connections and barriers. Tools like Jepsen and "Elle" find isolation bugs in whole databases.

Everyday analogy. Take-a-number tickets (atomic) versus everyone peeking at the queue and guessing who is next (check-then-act).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to Serializable when a single conditional UPDATE solves it.
  • Not stating the level you assume in the answer.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew (plus lost update).
  • Postgres: Read Uncommitted = Read Committed; Repeatable Read = snapshot isolation (no phantoms, but write skew possible); Serializable = SSI.
  • Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read per transaction.
  • Write skew breaks a shared invariant through different rows; fix with Serializable, FOR UPDATE on what you read, a guard row or a constraint.
  • Serializable and Repeatable Read writes can fail with 40001; always retry the whole transaction.
  • Atomic conditional UPDATE often beats a stronger isolation level.
  • MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read, Postgres to Read Committed; know the difference when migrating.

questions.promptHtml: What are the SQL isolation levels, and does Postgres implement them the way the standard describes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorised the standard's table from people who know what their actual database does.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Isolation controls how much of other running transactions I can see. The standard defines four levels, Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable, by which anomalies they forbid. Postgres deviates: Read Uncommitted is just Read Committed, Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation so it also blocks phantoms, and only Serializable, which uses SSI, blocks write skew. The default is Read Committed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each level trades anomalies for concurrency. Stronger means fewer anomalies but more blocking or more aborts.

Level (standard)      Dirty  NonRepeat  Phantom  WriteSkew
Read Uncommitted      yes    yes        yes      yes
Read Committed        no     yes        yes      yes
Repeatable Read       no     no         yes*     yes
Serializable          no     no         no       no
* Postgres RR is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew still possible.

Postgres is MVCC based, so a reader always sees a committed snapshot; dirty reads are structurally impossible. Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read and Serializable take one per transaction. Other engines differ: MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, Oracle only has Read Committed and a snapshot-based "Serializable", CockroachDB and Spanner are serializable by default.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SHOW transaction_isolation;
COMMIT;
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;  -- read committed

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reciting the standard table as if every engine follows it.
  • Saying Postgres defaults to Repeatable Read (that is MySQL).
  • Believing Repeatable Read in Postgres allows phantoms.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Read Uncommitted do in Postgres? -> Behaves exactly as Read Committed; no dirty reads ever.
  2. Is the level per connection or per transaction? -> Either; it can be set per transaction, per session or as a default, and per transaction is the safest habit.
  3. Which level would you pick for a financial ledger? -> Read Committed with atomic SQL or FOR UPDATE for simple paths, Serializable plus retries for check-then-act invariants; I state the level every critical path assumes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the four levels and anomalies. The senior adds engine-specific behaviour (snapshot per statement vs per transaction, MySQL differences), and that the real design question is which invariant needs which mechanism.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams migrating MySQL to Postgres discover code relied on InnoDB gap locks at Repeatable Read and silently lose protection at Postgres Read Committed.

questions.promptHtml: What is a dirty read, and can it happen in Postgres?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks the basic anomaly vocabulary and the Postgres-specific truth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A dirty read is seeing another transaction's uncommitted write. If that transaction rolls back, I acted on data that never existed. Postgres never allows it, even if I ask for Read Uncommitted, because readers only see committed row versions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Session A                          Session B
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=500
  WHERE id=1;
                                   BEGIN;
                                   SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1;
                                   -- Postgres: 100 (dirty-read DB: 500)
ROLLBACK;

In MVCC, A's new tuple has an xmin that is not committed, so B's snapshot treats it as invisible. SQL Server with READ UNCOMMITTED or NOLOCK really can show 500, plus duplicated or missing rows during page splits, because it reads without locks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;  -- accepted
SHOW transaction_isolation;                        -- read uncommitted, behaves as read committed

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking READ UNCOMMITTED gives dirty reads in Postgres.
  • Confusing dirty read (uncommitted) with stale read (committed but old).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would anyone want dirty reads? -> Cheap approximate reports on lock-based engines; pointless under MVCC where reads never block.
  2. Is a read from a replica a dirty read? -> No, it is a stale read; data is committed, just lagging.
  3. How does Postgres decide visibility? -> Snapshot of committed xids against tuple xmin/xmax.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "reading uncommitted data". Senior: explains the visibility mechanism and the NOLOCK reporting bugs on other engines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: SQL Server reports with NOLOCK showed revenue including later-cancelled orders; moving to snapshot isolation fixed it.

questions.subtopic: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read snapshots
questions.promptHtml: Explain a non-repeatable read and how Read Committed and Repeatable Read differ in Postgres.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Statement-level vs transaction-level snapshot is the core Postgres distinction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in a transaction and getting different committed values. In Read Committed every statement gets a fresh snapshot, so it can happen. In Repeatable Read the snapshot is taken at the first statement and held until the end, so both reads return the same value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A (Read Committed)                 B
BEGIN;
SELECT balance ... id=1;  -- 100
                                   UPDATE accounts SET balance=50 WHERE id=1; -- autocommit
SELECT balance ... id=1;  -- 50
COMMIT;

Under Repeatable Read, A's second select still returns 100. A subtle twist: in Read Committed, an UPDATE that has to wait on a row lock re-evaluates the WHERE on the newest committed version (EvalPlanQual), then applies to it. So SET balance = balance - 10 is safe, but read in app, compute, then SET balance = 90 loses updates.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
-- B commits a change here
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;  -- same as before
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Read Committed protects app-side read-modify-write.
  • Forgetting that a Repeatable Read writer can fail with could not serialize access due to concurrent update.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is the RR snapshot taken? -> At the first statement, not at BEGIN.
  2. What error does a conflicting RR write give? -> SQLSTATE 40001; retry the whole transaction.
  3. Why is SET x = x - 10 safe in Read Committed? -> The row lock plus re-check applies it to the latest version.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definition only. Senior: explains per-statement snapshots, EvalPlanQual and the lost-update angle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Multi-statement reports in Read Committed produced totals that did not match their own line items until moved to Repeatable Read READ ONLY.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service runs on Postgres at the default isolation. Support reports that when a user taps "redeem 20 points" twice quickly, only one deduction is recorded, but two rewards were issued. Traffic is 300 req/s. The handler:

def redeem(conn, user_id, cost):
    with conn.transaction():
        pts = conn.execute("SELECT points FROM wallet WHERE user_id=%s", (user_id,)).fetchone()[0]
        if pts < cost:
            raise Insufficient()
        conn.execute("UPDATE wallet SET points=%s WHERE user_id=%s", (pts - cost, user_id))
        grant_reward(conn, user_id)

A log excerpt: T1 read 100, T2 read 100, T1 write 80, T2 write 80. Your colleague blames the connection pool.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and fix it. What are your options?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in a transaction" (it already is), or "use Serializable" without explaining why a simpler fix exists, or blaming the pool.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the isolation level the default? (Yes, Read Committed.) Is points only changed here? (Other writers matter for the fix.) Is the reward side effect inside the transaction? (Needs rollback safety.) Is a double tap a client bug or expected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the redeem button server-side with an idempotency key; reconcile affected wallets from the reward ledger.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) read-modify-write race in Read Committed; (b) duplicate request from the client (a red herring that makes it worse, not the cause); (c) pool problem, unlikely because both transactions committed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log shows both read 100 before either write, which is the lost update signature. Reproduce with two psql sessions and pg_sleep between read and write.
  5. Root cause: Read Committed gives each statement its own snapshot and takes no lock on read. Both transactions computed 80 from stale 100 and the second overwrote the first.
  6. Fix: Short-term, atomic conditional update:
UPDATE wallet SET points = points - 20
WHERE user_id = 7 AND points >= 20
RETURNING points;   -- 0 rows = insufficient

Long-term, if logic is complex, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first, or a version column. 7. Prevention: Code review rule against read in app then write absolute value; a concurrency test with two connections; idempotency key on redeem. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Serializable here; it would work but adds retries when one atomic statement suffices.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the cost depends on a rule engine in code? -> Use FOR UPDATE on the wallet row, then compute and write.
  • What if the app uses Repeatable Read? -> The second writer errors with 40001; add a retry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A loyalty program issued thousands of duplicate rewards at a promotion peak. The code had always been racy; load only exposed it. The atomic UPDATE with RETURNING closed it with a four-line diff.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames pool or adds more transactions.
  • Hire: identifies the lost update, uses FOR UPDATE or atomic UPDATE.
  • Strong hire: also covers RR retry behaviour, idempotency and a test that reproduces the race.

questions.promptHtml: What is a phantom read, how does it differ from a non-repeatable read, and how do Postgres and MySQL prevent it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can distinguish row-level from set-level anomalies and know engine-specific mechanisms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A non-repeatable read is a row I already saw changing. A phantom is the set of rows matching a predicate changing, a new row appearing or one vanishing. Row locks cannot stop it because the new row did not exist to lock. Postgres Repeatable Read prevents it with the snapshot; InnoDB uses next-key (gap) locks for locking reads.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A                                  B
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE day='2026-11-09';  -- 10
                                   INSERT INTO orders(day) VALUES ('2026-11-09'); COMMIT;
SELECT count(*) ... ;  -- RC: 11 (phantom)   RR in Postgres: 10

The standard permits phantoms at Repeatable Read, but a snapshot hides everything committed after it, so Postgres RR is stronger. InnoDB RR gives snapshot reads for plain SELECT, but SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and writes read the latest data and take gap locks, so mixed code can still observe surprises.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing up phantom and non-repeatable read.
  • Claiming Postgres RR has phantoms.
  • Assuming a snapshot prevents the write-side consequences (see write skew).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the snapshot stop an insert that violates a rule I checked? -> No; that is write skew, needing Serializable or a lock.
  2. What is a gap lock? -> InnoDB lock on the range between index entries, blocking inserts into it.
  3. What does Postgres use for predicate-level protection? -> SSI SIREAD locks under Serializable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definition. Senior: engine differences, and that snapshot reads do not protect decisions based on the set.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A quota check count(*) < limit then insert passed under both RC and RR snapshots, letting two concurrent requests exceed the limit.

questions.contextHtml: A nightly finance export runs five queries (totals by day, by region, by merchant, refunds, row count) on Postgres at the default level while ~800 orders/s are inserted. Finance complains the five numbers never reconcile: the row count is higher than the sum of regional counts by 40-300. The export takes 4 minutes. The team proposes locking the orders table.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the discrepancy and propose a fix without hurting writers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lock the table during export" (outage) or "run the queries in a transaction" with no level named (still Read Committed, same bug).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Replica or primary? Must all numbers be as of a single instant? Is 4 minutes of snapshot age acceptable? Any long-transaction alarms?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-run the export on a consistent snapshot; no table lock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Read Committed gives each statement a new snapshot, so inserts between statements cause drift; (b) rows updated between statements; (c) a replica lag red herring, which gives stale but still self-consistent data per statement.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the row count twice in one transaction and compare; check SHOW transaction_isolation.
  5. Root cause: Set-level drift: phantoms across statements.
  6. Fix:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;
SELECT ...; -- all five queries
COMMIT;

All five see one snapshot, writers are never blocked. Use pg_export_snapshot if parallel workers must share it. 7. Prevention: Make the export wrapper set the level; monitor transaction age, because a 4 minute snapshot holds back vacuum. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not table locks. Not Serializable; a read-only report gains nothing. Prefer a replica to avoid vacuum horizon impact, accepting max_standby_streaming_delay conflicts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Export runs 3 hours? -> Snapshot holds vacuum back; use a replica or partitioned incremental exports.
  • Need parallel dump workers? -> Export the snapshot id to each worker.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reconciliation job mismatched by tiny amounts for months; blamed rounding. It was phantom drift across queries, fixed by one line setting the level.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: locks tables.
  • Hire: Repeatable Read READ ONLY single transaction.
  • Strong hire: adds vacuum horizon cost, snapshot export for parallelism, replica option.

questions.promptHtml: What is write skew? Show an example and give several ways to prevent it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the anomaly that snapshot isolation misses, common in real invariants.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Two transactions read overlapping data, each concludes an action is safe, and each writes a different row. There is no write-write conflict, so snapshot isolation allows both, but together they break an invariant. Prevent it with Serializable plus retry, with FOR UPDATE on the rows I read, with a shared guard row, or with a constraint.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hospital rule: at least one doctor on call.

A (RR)                              B (RR)
BEGIN;                              BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call; -- 2
                                    SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call; -- 2
UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false WHERE name='Alice';
                                    UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false WHERE name='Bob';
COMMIT;                             COMMIT;   -- both succeed, zero on call

Postgres's first-updater-wins check only fires when two transactions touch the same row. Different rows, no conflict.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- option: lock what you read
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM doctors WHERE on_call FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Alice';
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing Repeatable Read protects check-then-act.
  • Serializable without retry.
  • FOR UPDATE on only the row being modified, not the rows read.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does FOR UPDATE on the read set work? -> The second transaction waits, then re-evaluates and sees the first change.
  2. Can a constraint help? -> Sometimes, like EXCLUDE for overlapping bookings; counting rules usually cannot.
  3. Does it happen in Read Committed? -> Yes, even easier.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: gives the doctor example. Senior: lists the four prevention choices with their costs and knows which to pick per workload.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-booked meeting rooms and oversold last seats are all write skew.

questions.contextHtml: A team moves a ticket-allocation service from MySQL InnoDB (default Repeatable Read) to Postgres (default Read Committed). The code does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE event_id=? AND status='sold', then inserts a sale if below capacity. In MySQL staging they never oversold. After cutover at 1,200 req/s, event 311 (capacity 500) shows 507 sold. Nobody changed the SQL. Logs show no errors and no deadlocks.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the behaviour change and how do you fix it safely during live traffic?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to Repeatable Read in Postgres because MySQL used it". That does not reproduce InnoDB's gap locking, and writes still race.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the MySQL code use a plain SELECT or a locking read? Is there a unique key on (event, seat)? Are sales inserts only from this service? Is oversell recoverable (refunds)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause sales for that event or cap at a conservative number, refund the 7 extras.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-insert race that InnoDB masked (likely the original code was FOR UPDATE or gap-locked, and ORM changes dropped it); (b) a read replica serving the count (red herring unless reads go there); (c) clock or retry duplication.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run two psql sessions with a pg_sleep between count and insert to reproduce; grep the query path for FOR UPDATE.
  5. Root cause: Read Committed plus plain count gives no mutual exclusion. Even Repeatable Read would still permit this as write skew; InnoDB prevented it only through locking reads taking gap locks.
  6. Fix: Short-term: an atomic guard using a per-event counter row:
UPDATE events SET sold = sold + 1
WHERE id = 311 AND sold < capacity
RETURNING sold;   -- 0 rows = sold out

then insert the ticket in the same transaction. Long-term: Serializable with retries only if the rule cannot be expressed as a counter. 7. Prevention: A migration checklist for isolation-dependent code, concurrency tests in staging with N parallel buyers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The counter row is a hot row; if one event gets 10k req/s, shard or queue it. I would not rely on RR.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Counter row contention? -> Pre-allocate inventory tokens or shard counters, reconcile.
  • Why not a unique constraint? -> Works for numbered seats, not for "count under capacity".

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration passed all functional tests because staging was single-threaded. The first big on-sale found the race in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "set RR".
  • Hire: explains write skew, atomic counter or FOR UPDATE.
  • Strong hire: explains InnoDB gap lock difference, hot-row mitigation and a migration checklist.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks: "usernames must be unique, case-insensitive". The signup handler runs SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE lower(name)=lower($1), and if no row, INSERT INTO users(name, ...). At 40 signups/s it has worked for a year. During a marketing campaign (400 signups/s) support finds two accounts, Priya and priya. The table has a plain unique index on name. A teammate says "just use Serializable".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what is the cheapest correct fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Serializable everywhere, or an app-level in-memory lock (fails with multiple instances).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I change the schema? How many existing duplicates? Is Unicode normalisation required? Is signup one instance or many?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Merge or rename the duplicate accounts; enable a lock via pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(lower($1))) as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-insert race; (b) the unique index is case-sensitive so it does not cover priya; (c) a replica read (red herring: the check reads primary).
  4. How I'd verify each: Two psql sessions inserting Priya and priya with pg_sleep between check and insert; \d users shows the index definition.
  5. Root cause: The invariant lives in code, not the database. Both checks saw nothing, and inserts of different keys do not conflict.
  6. Fix:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_name_lower_uq ON users (lower(name));
-- app: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, treat 0 rows as "taken"

Clean duplicates first or the build fails. 7. Prevention: Rule: every uniqueness rule must be a constraint; a review checklist item. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Serializable; a constraint is cheaper, deterministic and has no retries. Advisory locks stay only as a temporary patch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Uniqueness across two tables? -> A shared registry table with a unique key, or EXCLUDE; otherwise Serializable.
  • Concurrent index build fails midway? -> Leaves an INVALID index; drop and retry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "rare" duplicate-email bug took a week to find because it only appeared during promotions. The fix was a one-line index.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: in-memory lock or Serializable only.
  • Hire: unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT.
  • Strong hire: also handles duplicates cleanup, concurrent index build and normalisation.

questions.promptHtml: How does Postgres implement Serializable, and what must the application do to use it correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth: understanding it aborts rather than blocks, and the operational consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Postgres uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation. Transactions run on snapshots without extra blocking, while the engine tracks read-write dependencies with SIREAD predicate locks. When it sees a dangerous structure, two consecutive rw-dependencies, it aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001. The application must retry the whole transaction.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A SIREAD lock records what a transaction read, but does not block anyone. If another transaction writes something that read overlaps, an rw-edge is recorded. A cycle in the dependency graph means no serial order explains the result; the tell-tale pattern is T1 -rw-> T2 -rw-> T3 with T3 committing first. The engine is conservative, so false positives occur.

Tx A reads set S          -> SIREAD locks on S
Tx B writes into S        -> rw-edge A->B
Tx B reads T, Tx A writes -> rw-edge B->A  => dangerous: abort one (40001)

Operational facts: predicate locks start at tuple granularity and are promoted to page then relation level when max_pred_locks_per_transaction (default 64) runs short, which increases false aborts. A sequential scan takes a relation-level SIREAD lock, so missing indexes raise abort rates. Long read-only work can use READ ONLY DEFERRABLE. All transactions in the invariant must be Serializable for protection.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        with conn.transaction():          # BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
            do_work(conn)
        break
    except SerializationFailure:           # 40001
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.01 * 2**attempt))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No retry, so users see 500s.
  • Retrying only the failed statement instead of the whole transaction.
  • External side effects (emails, payments) inside the retried block.
  • Mixing levels and expecting full protection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Serializable take table locks? -> No; it aborts rather than blocks.
  2. Why do missing indexes hurt? -> Seq scans take coarse SIREAD locks, so more false conflicts.
  3. How do you keep long reports from being aborted? -> READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits for a safe snapshot, then never aborts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Serializable is slow and locks everything". Senior: no blocking, abort-based, retry design, side-effect idempotency and the predicate-lock tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled Serializable globally and saw 40001 climb from 0 to 8% at peak because scans lacked indexes and predicate locks escalated.

questions.contextHtml:
A flash-sale seat service sells 100,000 seats, launch traffic 5,000 req/s, many people fighting for the same popular seats. The booking transaction today is Serializable with a retry loop: it reads SELECT holder FROM seats WHERE id=$1, checks null, then updates. At 500 req/s in the last event it worked. In the load test at 5,000 req/s:

p50 40 ms, p99 2.8 s
pg_stat_database xact_rollback: 38% of transactions
app log: ERROR could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies (40001)
retries per request avg 3.4, max 5 then 500

CPU on the DB is 55%.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change, and what would you tell product about the design trade-off?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raise retry count and add more DB CPU.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a seat contested by many users at once (hot rows)? Does a booking touch more than one seat? Is payment inside the transaction? What is acceptable failure rate for losing contenders?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap retries with jitter, shed load with a queue or waiting room.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) contention: many transactions racing for the same row, retries amplify load; (b) false positives from coarse predicate locks (seq scan, page promotion); (c) CPU is not saturated, so it is not a capacity problem (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Check the EXPLAIN plan for index use; compare abort rate against concurrent attempts per seat; inspect pg_locks for SIReadLock counts.
  5. Root cause: Serializable correctly aborts losers of a read-then-write race on hot rows; at 10x the aborts retry and re-contend, creating a retry storm.
  6. Fix:
UPDATE seats SET holder = $1
WHERE id = $2 AND holder IS NULL
RETURNING id;     -- 1 row = booked, 0 rows = lost

At Read Committed, one statement, no retries; the loser gets an immediate "taken". The update re-checks after waiting. 7. Prevention: Load test with contention patterns, not just uniform keys; alert on xact_rollback ratio and 40001 count. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would keep Serializable only for multi-row invariants (for example "max 4 seats per user") or move those to a guard row. Not raising retry counts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Booking must also decrement a per-user quota? -> Same transaction with a conditional UPDATE on the quota row.
  • Hold seats for 10 minutes? -> A held_until column in the same conditional update.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day abort storm looked like a DB problem; the fix was deleting the check-then-write pattern, reducing p99 from seconds to 30 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tune retries and hardware.
  • Hire: atomic conditional UPDATE at Read Committed.
  • Strong hire: explains retry amplification, predicate lock escalation and where Serializable still fits.

questions.contextHtml:
A team protects the "at most 3 active projects per workspace" rule with Serializable in the API path create_project. Violations still occur (workspace 88 has 5). Code review shows:

# api path
with conn.transaction(isolation="serializable"):
    n = conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM projects WHERE ws=%s AND active", (ws,)).fetchone()[0]
    if n >= 3: raise Limit()
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO projects(ws, active) VALUES (%s, true)", (ws,))

# import job (batch, default isolation)
conn.execute("INSERT INTO projects(ws, active) SELECT %s, true FROM staging WHERE ...", (ws,))

Postgres log shows no 40001 for workspace 88.
questions.promptHtml: Why does Serializable not protect the rule? Fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Serializable is broken" or "add more retries".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which code paths write projects? Can the import be rerouted through the API? Is the limit a hard business rule?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the import for affected workspaces; archive extras per product rules.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the import runs below Serializable, so SSI never tracks it; (b) a race between two API calls (would give 40001, which we do not see); (c) a replica read (red herring: writes go to primary).
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep all INSERT/UPDATE paths on projects; check application_name and isolation in pg_stat_activity; test API-vs-import interleaving in two sessions.
  5. Root cause: SSI only tracks dependencies among Serializable transactions. A non-Serializable writer inserts without leaving or checking SIREAD dependencies.
  6. Fix: Run the import also at Serializable (with retries), or make every path go through one function that locks a guard row SELECT ... FROM workspaces WHERE id=$1 FOR UPDATE before counting.
  7. Prevention: Single write path per invariant; a test that interleaves API and batch; lint for raw inserts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The guard row serialises per workspace only, cheap and explicit. A trigger could enforce it but hides the cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Import has 10M rows? -> Batch it per workspace, under the guard lock.
  • Could a CHECK constraint do this? -> No; it cannot see other rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "serializable" system leaked because a back-office script used autocommit. After that, every invariant had one named owner function.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the database.
  • Hire: all participants must be Serializable, or lock a guard row.
  • Strong hire: audits every write path and adds an interleaving test.

questions.contextHtml:
After a deploy that set default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable' for a 6-node API fleet, error rate climbs. Metrics:

5xx: 0.2% -> 4.7% in 20 minutes
Postgres log: ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
              HINT: The transaction might succeed if retried.
pg_locks: 410k rows of mode SIReadLock, 'relation' granularity on orders
shared memory warning: out of shared memory (max_pred_locks_per_transaction)

Only the orders service has retry logic. A big nightly-style report query is running during business hours.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Roll back and call Serializable bad, or increase pool size.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints fail? Is the report query seq-scanning orders? Do callers retry? Rollback is safe only if no code relies on Serializable.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the default to Read Committed (per-role or per-database setting), keeping Serializable only where the code retries and relies on it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) services without retries now see 40001 as 5xx; (b) report seq scan creates relation-level SIREAD locks conflicting with all writers; (c) too small max_pred_locks_per_transaction; (d) a deadlock (red herring: that would be 40P01).
  4. How I'd verify each: Group errors by endpoint; SELECT mode, granularity, count(*) FROM pg_locks WHERE mode='SIReadLock' GROUP BY 1,2; EXPLAIN the report.
  5. Root cause: A blanket global change without app support. Reports are long readers with coarse predicate locks; they generate dangerous structures and the engine aborts conservatively.
  6. Fix: Short-term: revert default, move reports to READ ONLY DEFERRABLE or a replica. Long-term: opt in per transaction only for invariant-guarding paths, with a shared retry helper, indexes to keep predicate locks fine-grained, and idempotent side effects.
  7. Prevention: Canary on one node; dashboard of 40001 per route; load test with reports running.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising max_pred_locks_per_transaction blindly; it uses shared memory and hides missing indexes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can't revert quickly? -> Set the role default for the report user to read committed.
  • What if retry causes duplicated emails? -> Move side effects after commit via an outbox.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meaning "make it safer" config change took a day to unwind. The lasting rule: isolation changes are code changes, shipped with retry and tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rolls back, no root cause.
  • Hire: ties errors to missing retries and report scans.
  • Strong hire: per-transaction opt-in, DEFERRABLE reports, outbox for side effects, canary.

questions.contextHtml: Postmortem: a meeting-room booking service double-booked room R7 for 14:00. Two requests arrived 3 ms apart. Code does SELECT ... WHERE room=? AND tstzrange overlaps then inserts. Unit tests passed; staging never reproduced it. The incident review asks for (1) a root cause, (2) a fix that prevents recurrence in the database, and (3) a test that would have caught it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a retry and more logging" with no test or DB-level guard.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the time range stored as a range type? Are bookings ever cancelled (soft delete)? Is the table large? Do other writers exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Contact the two bookers; manually resolve; add the guard below.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) write skew: both checks saw no overlap; (b) clock skew (red herring: the requests overlapped in real time); (c) duplicate message delivery.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with two sessions and pg_sleep(2) between check and insert; check request ids in logs.
  5. Root cause: An application check-then-insert on a range invariant; snapshot isolation does not conflict on inserts of different rows.
  6. Fix:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
  WHERE (NOT cancelled);

The database now rejects the second insert with 23P01; the app maps that to "room taken". 7. Prevention: The test: two connections, a barrier, both insert overlapping ranges, assert exactly one succeeds, run 200 iterations; add a pg_sleep hook to widen the window. Consider Jepsen-style randomised testing for critical flows.

def test_no_double_booking(db):
    barrier = threading.Barrier(2)
    results = []
    def attempt():
        with db.conn() as c:
            barrier.wait()
            results.append(book(c, "R7", "14:00-15:00"))
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=attempt) for _ in range(2)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    assert results.count(True) == 1
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not relying on Serializable alone; an exclusion constraint is cheaper and permanent. Not skipping the test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Constraint needs deferred checking? -> EXCLUDE can be DEFERRABLE.
  • Multi-room bookings atomic? -> One transaction; constraint still holds per row.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The same defect was found in three other services after the review by grepping for check-then-insert; one constraint per invariant ended the class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries and logging only.
  • Hire: exclusion or unique constraint, two-session reproduction.
  • Strong hire: automated barrier test, review of sibling code, constraint error mapping.
